questions.questionText:
**Passage:**
The school library had been neglected for several years. Books were dusty, some shelves were broken and many learners preferred to spend their free time outside. A new librarian decided to change the situation. She organised the books, repaired the shelves with the help of the school maintenance team and started a reading club. Within a few months, learners were borrowing books regularly and discussing stories during break time.

Read the passage carefully. Answer the questions that follow. Passage 1.
- (a) Give one reason why the learners initially avoided the library. [1 mark]
- (b) State two actions taken by the new librarian. [2 marks]
- (c) What evidence shows that the changes were successful? [2 marks]
- (d) Give a suitable title for the passage. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Comprehension Answers [6 marks]:** **(a)** Learners initially avoided the library because the books were covered in dust and several bookshelves were broken [1 mark]. **(b)** The new librarian took three decisive actions (any two required): she sorted and organised the books neatly, worked with the school maintenance team to repair broken shelves, and launched a reading club [2 marks]. **(c)** Two pieces of evidence prove the revival succeeded: within a few months learners began borrowing books regularly and discussing stories enthusiastically during break time [2 marks]. **(d)** A suitable concise title reflecting the central idea is **"Reviving the School Library"** or **"The New Librarian’s Transformation"** [1 mark].

Notice how every answer above demonstrates proper **ZIMSEC 7010/2 full-sentence comprehension technique**: rather than writing fragmented phrases such as "dusty books", restating the question stem (*"Learners initially avoided the library because..."*) keeps subject-verb agreement intact and earns guaranteed marks. In part (b), counting the exact command number (**"two actions"**) stops you from wasting precious minutes copying a third extra point when the mark scheme caps part (b) at 2 marks.

A common national error in Paper 2 passage comprehension is wholesale copying ("lifting") of long lines containing irrelevant facts. Always read every clue carefully, select only the exact evidence answering *why*, *what actions*, or *what proof*, and keep titles short (3–6 words without ending punctuation).

questions.questionText:
Rewrite the sentence in the plural: 'The child carried a box to the classroom.'
- (a) Rewrite the sentence correctly in the plural. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Grammar Answer [2 marks]:** Converted correctly into plural form, the sentence becomes: **"The children carried boxes to the classrooms."** [2 marks]. Notice every countable noun changes simultaneously while the past-tense verb remains unchanged: **child → children** (irregular plural—never write "childs"), **a box → boxes** (adding **-es** after **-x** and dropping the singular indefinite article **a**), and **classroom → classrooms** (regular **-s** plural).

In English grammar, converting a sentence from singular to plural demands checking three things systematically from left to right: **(1) determiners/articles** (*a* or *an* cannot appear before plural countable nouns, so drop *a* or change to *some/the*), **(2) irregular and regular noun endings** (*child → children*, *box → boxes* following the *-s, -sh, -ch, -x, -z → -es* rule), and **(3) verb tense agreement** (since **carried** is simple past tense, it stays identical for both singular *"the child carried"* and plural *"the children carried"*).

Grade 7 markers regularly penalise two classic mistakes: writing *"childrens"* or *"the children carried a boxes"* (forgetting to delete **a** before the plural **boxes**), or leaving **"the classroom"** singular while pluralising the rest. Check every noun one by one before writing your final sentence.

questions.questionText:
Correct the error in the sentence: 'Neither of the boys have completed the task.'
- (a) Write the corrected sentence. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Grammar Correction [2 marks]:** The grammatically corrected sentence is: **"Neither of the boys has completed the task."** [2 marks]. The error lies in the plural verb **"have"**, which must be replaced with the singular auxiliary verb **"has"** because the distributive pronoun **"Neither"** refers to *not one individual boy* out of the pair and always governs a singular verb.

Many learners get tricked by the plural noun **"boys"** standing right beside the verb inside the prepositional phrase *"of the boys"*. Remember the ZIMSEC subject-verb concord rule: words such as **each, either, neither, everyone, somebody, and nobody** act strictly as singular subjects regardless of any plural nouns inside *"of the ..."* (for instance: *"Neither of the girls **is** absent"*, *"Each of the learners **was** given a ruler"*).

When answering error-correction items in Paper 2, write out the **complete corrected sentence** neatly rather than circling or writing just the single word *"has"* unless specifically told otherwise—and read aloud mentally with *"Neither one..."* to verify smooth singular agreement.

questions.questionText:
Join the sentences using 'although': 'The road was muddy. The bus continued its journey.'
- (a) Write one correct combined sentence. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Conjunction Answer [2 marks]:** Combined smoothly using the subordinating conjunction **"although"**, the correct sentence is: **"Although the road was muddy, the bus continued its journey."** (Equally valid: **"The bus continued its journey although the road was muddy."**) [2 marks].

**Although** expresses **concession / contrast** between two clauses where the second outcome happens unexpectedly despite an obstacle in the first clause—unlike *because* (cause) or *and* (addition). Grammar punctuation matters too: when the subordinate *Although...* clause comes **first**, place a **comma** cleanly after *"muddy,"* before starting the main clause (*"the bus continued its journey"*); when *although* sits in the middle between clauses, no comma is usually needed.

The commonest ZIMSEC error when combining sentences with *although* is leaving **"but"** inside the same sentence (*"Although the road was muddy, but the bus continued"*—wrong! Never pair *although* with *but*!). Use **either** *although* **or** *but*, never both together.

questions.questionText:
Rewrite the sentence in the past tense: 'The learners clean the classroom every Friday.'
- (a) Write the sentence in the past tense. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Tense Answer [2 marks]:** Rewritten accurately in the **simple past tense**, the sentence reads: **"The learners cleaned the classroom every Friday."** (Or referring to a specific past occasion: *"The learners cleaned the classroom last Friday."*) [2 marks]. The regular present-tense verb **"clean"** adds **-ed** to form the simple past **"cleaned"** while keeping the rest of the sentence intact.

Changing tenses in ZIMSEC language sections focuses sharply on identifying the **finite verb** carrying time: in *"The learners clean..."*, plural subject *learners* pairs with base form *clean* indicating a present habit. Switching to simple past requires **-ed** on regular verbs (*clean → cleaned*)—never adding unnecessary helping words like *"were cleaned"* (passive!) or *"did cleaned"* (double past!).

Always verify spelling and voice: writing *"The learners were clean"* changes the meaning into an adjective instead of a past action, whereas **The learners cleaned the classroom every Friday** preserves active subject-action meaning cleanly.

questions.questionText:
Replace the underlined noun phrase with a suitable pronoun: 'Rudo and Chipo carried the books.'
- (a) Rewrite the sentence using an appropriate pronoun. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Pronoun Answer [2 marks]:** Replacing the compound plural noun phrase **"Rudo and Chipo"** with the matching subject pronoun yields: **"They carried the books."** [2 marks]. Because Rudo and Chipo together form a **third-person plural subject** performing the action (*carried*), the correct nominative plural pronoun is **"They"** (never *"Them"* or *"She"*).

Pronoun substitution in Grade 7 grammar requires testing both **number** (one person vs two or more people) and **grammatical case** (**subject** vs **object**). When replacing the doer before the verb (*"Rudo and Chipo carried..."*), choose subject pronoun **They**; had their names appeared *after* a verb or preposition (*"The teacher praised Rudo and Chipo"*), you would choose object pronoun **them** (*"The teacher praised them"*).

Learners occasionally write ungrammatical dialect forms like *"Them carried the books"* or *"They two carried"*. Always capitalise **They** at the start of the sentence and read it back carefully to confirm crisp standard English.

questions.questionText:
Rewrite using 'not only...but also': 'The club teaches reading. The club teaches writing.'
- (a) Write the combined sentence. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Correlative Conjunction Answer [2 marks]:** Joined cleanly using **"not only ... but also"**, the sentence becomes: **"The club teaches not only reading but also writing."** [2 marks]. Notice that parallel grammatical items—two gerund nouns (**reading** and **writing**)—follow immediately after *"not only"* and *"but also"* without repeating *"The club teaches"* twice unnecessarily.

The correlative pair **not only … but also …** emphasises that two balanced facts are both true. To maintain **parallel structure**, place *"not only"* right before the first differing element (*reading*) rather than too early (*"Not only the club teaches reading"* shifts subject position awkwardly): keep the shared opening **"The club teaches"** once, then link **not only [Item 1] but also [Item 2]**.

ZIMSEC markers deduct marks if candidates misspell **"also"** or write *"not only reading, but writing too"* missing the required **"but also"** phrase, or leave both sentences loosely fused with a comma. Double-check exact parallel balance around **"not only"** and **"but also"**.

questions.questionText:
Change the direct speech into reported speech: 'I am ready,' Tendai said.
- (a) Write the sentence in reported speech. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Reported Speech Answer [2 marks]:** Changed accurately from direct speech into **reported (indirect) speech**, the sentence becomes: **"Tendai said that he was ready."** (Or **"Tendai said that she was ready."**) [2 marks]. Notice all four required adjustments: remove quotation marks and comma, add optional reporting conjunction **"that"**, shift pronoun **"I" → "he/she"**, and backshift present tense **"am" → past tense "was"**.

Reported speech shifts a speaker’s exact spoken words (**"I am ready"**) back in time from the narrator’s perspective after a past reporting verb (**said**). Because the speaker is Tendai, first-person *"I"* becomes third-person **he** or **she**, and present linking verb *"am"* steps back one tense into **was**—while retaining the speaker’s exact meaning cleanly without speech marks.

The top Grade 7 errors in reported speech are forgetting to remove quotation marks ('Tendai said that "he was ready"'—wrong!) or failing to backshift the verb ('Tendai said that he is ready'). Always verify **zero speech marks**, **pronoun match**, and **past-tense backshift ('am → was')**.

questions.questionText:
Add the missing punctuation: 'what a beautiful garden said the visitor'
- (a) Rewrite the sentence with correct punctuation. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Punctuation Answer [2 marks]:** Rewritten with accurate capitalisation, quotation marks, and end-of-quote exclamation/punctuation, the sentence reads: **"What a beautiful garden!" said the visitor.** (Also acceptable: *"What a beautiful garden," said the visitor.*) [2 marks]. Notice **W** is capitalised at the start of direct speech, opening/closing inverted commas **'"..."'** wrap ONLY the spoken words, an exclamation mark **'!'** (or comma) sits *inside* the closing quotation mark before *"said"*, and a full stop ends the reporting clause after **visitor.**

Punctuating direct speech cleanly separates **what was actually spoken aloud** from **who spoke it**. Because *"What a beautiful garden!"* expresses strong admiration beginning with exclamatory *"What a..."*, an exclamation mark inside the closing inverted commas ('!"') captures tone far better than a bare comma, yet *"said"* still begins with a lowercase **s** because *"said the visitor"* finishes the same single grammatical sentence!

Candidates routinely lose punctuation marks in Paper 2 by forgetting either opening/closing speech marks, missing the closing **full stop after 'visitor.'**, or mistakenly capitalising 'Said' after an exclamation mark inside dialogue. Inspect every boundary carefully.

questions.questionText:
Give an antonym for the underlined word: 'The water was shallow.'
- (a) Write the opposite of 'shallow'. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Vocabulary Answer [1–2 marks]:** The direct antonym (word opposite in meaning) for **"shallow"** in *"The water was shallow"* is **"deep"** [1 mark]. Rewritten cleanly in context: **"The water was deep."**

An **antonym** contrasts opposite qualities along the same scale of meaning while keeping the **exact same part of speech**. Here *"shallow"* functions as a descriptive **adjective** describing low vertical depth of water; therefore its precise adjective opposite is **deep** (avoid loose phrases like *"not shallow"* or unrelated words like *"high"* or *"wide"*, which measure horizontal breadth or elevation rather than downward water depth!).

In ZIMSEC English Paper 2, check whether the instruction asks for a **single word opposite** (**deep**) or to **rewrite the whole sentence with the opposite**. Giving both the exact word (**deep**) and its contextual sentence guarantees zero lost marks.

questions.questionText:
Give a synonym for the underlined word: 'The villagers were delighted.'
- (a) Write one word with a similar meaning to 'delighted'. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Vocabulary Answer [1–2 marks]:** Accurate single-word **synonyms** (words closest in meaning) for **"delighted"** in *"The villagers were delighted"* are **"overjoyed"**, **"thrilled"**, **"pleased"**, **"glad"**, or **"happy"** [1 mark]. In context: **"The villagers were overjoyed."**

Choosing an accurate synonym means matching both **meaning intensity** and **grammatical word class**. Since *"delighted"* is a past-participle/adjective expressing warm great happiness, **overjoyed** or **thrilled** mirrors its strong positive intensity best, whereas **pleased** and **happy** also fit smoothly in standard Grade 7 grammar without changing tense or plural agreement (*"were overjoyed"*).

Never supply an explanatory phrase (like *"feeling good"*) when the exam specifically requests **one word** with a similar meaning—stick strictly to one crisp adjective (**overjoyed / thrilled / pleased**) that slots directly into *"The villagers were ____."*

questions.questionText:
Write a friendly letter to a cousin describing a memorable school event.
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Friendly Letter Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Follow official **ZIMSEC 7010/2 Informal (Friendly) Letter Format**: **(1) Top right:** Write ONE address only—your own street/school address with date below (e.g., *Mupfure Primary School, P.O. Box 42, Chegutu, 18 October 2026*) [3 marks]; **(2) Left margin:** Warm salutation (*"Dear Cousin Tatenda,"*) [1 mark]; **(3) Opening paragraph:** Friendly greeting asking about aunt, uncle, and cousin’s schoolwork before introducing your memorable event (for instance, Inter-House Athletics Day or Grade 7 Heritage Cultural Festival) [4 marks]; **(4) Body paragraphs (2–3 paragraphs):** Describe **when and where** it happened, **vivid sights and sounds** (drumming, cheering, winning the 4×100 m relay or cultural dance), and **how you felt** using expressive verbs and sensory adjectives [11 marks]; **(5) Warm closing & sign-off:** Brief farewell sending greetings home plus *"Your loving cousin, Chipo"* (first name only) [6 marks for layout close + grammar].

Keeping **consistent past tense** throughout your narrative (*cheered, sprinted, beamed, celebrated*) alongside lively dialogue or personal reflection makes a friendly letter sound natural, warm, and genuinely engaging rather than reading like a stiff list of times. Vary your sentence openings (*"As soon as the whistle blew...", "To my surprise..."*) and write comfortably around 120–150 focused words across 4 clear paragraphs.

Two big ZIMSEC Paper 2 traps sink otherwise strong friendly letters: accidentally writing **two addresses** (only *formal* letters use recipient addresses!), and signing off stiffly with *"Yours faithfully, Chipo Moyo"* instead of warm informal sign-offs (**"Your loving cousin,"** or **"Yours affectionately,"** + first name).

questions.questionText:
Write a formal letter to the head of your school suggesting two ways of improving the school grounds.
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Formal Letter Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Follow strict **ZIMSEC 7010/2 Formal Business Letter Format**: **(1) Top right / block format:** Your own sender’s address + date; **(2) Left margin:** Recipient’s official title & school address (*The Head, [School Name], P.O. Box ...*) [4 marks]; **(3) Salutation & Heading:** *"Dear Sir/Madam,"* followed by a **concise underlined/bold subject line** (*RE: SUGGESTIONS FOR IMPROVING THE SCHOOL GROUNDS*) [3 marks]; **(4) Focused Body Paragraphs:** Paragraph 1 states politely why you are writing as a concerned Grade 7 prefect/learner. Paragraph 2 explains **Suggestion 1** clearly (e.g., planting indigenous shade trees and flowerbeds around walkways with duty rosters so erosion and dust drop). Paragraph 3 explains **Suggestion 2** (e.g., placing labelled colour-coded litter bins and paved stone footpaths to stop mud being tracked into classrooms) [12 marks]; **(5) Polite close & full sign-off:** Hope-for-action closing followed by **"Yours faithfully,"** (when using *Sir/Madam*), handwritten signature, and your **full name** (**Tendai Moyo**) [6 marks].

Register in a formal letter must stay polite, respectful, persuasive, and free of slang or contractions (*write "cannot" and "it would improve" instead of "can't" or "wanna"*). Backing up each practical suggestion with clear benefits—cooler shade during breaks, cleaner classrooms, and proud visitors—persuades examiners you understand real problem-solving.

Markers frequently deduct layout marks when candidates omit the **recipient’s address**, forget **RE: SUBJECT HEADING**, write informal greetings (*"How are you, Headmaster?"*), or mix **"Dear Sir/Madam"** with **"Yours sincerely"** (remember: *Dear Sir/Madam → **Yours faithfully**; Dear Mr Moyo → **Yours sincerely***).

questions.questionText:
Write a story beginning with: 'When I opened the old wooden box, I could not believe what I saw.'
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Narrative Composition Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Begin **word-for-word** with the required opening sentence without altering a single punctuation mark: **"When I opened the old wooden box, I could not believe what I saw."** [2 marks]. **Paragraph 1 (Hook & Discovery):** Establish *where* you found the dusty box (e.g., cleaning Grandmother’s old storeroom during August holidays) and **reveal an intriguing, believable object inside**—such as a faded hand-carved soapstone bird wrapper, yellowed 1980 Independence newspaper clippings, or a brass pocket watch and family photographs [5 marks]. **Paragraphs 2–3 (Rising Mystery & Explanation):** Describe your amazement using vivid sensory clues (*creaking hinges, smell of cedarwood, trembling fingers*) and share how an elder/Grandmother entered and revealed the inspiring backstory connecting your family to perseverance or heritage [10 marks]. **Paragraph 4 (Reflection & Resolution):** End meaningfully explaining how guarding that heirloom taught gratitude and pride in family roots [8 marks for style & accuracy].

Strong Grade 7 stories stay **credible and tightly focused** around one brief afternoon scene rather than wandering into wild impossible adventures (avoid ending abruptly with *"and then I woke up from a dream"*—ZIMSEC markers penalise cliché dream endings!). Using strong descriptive verbs (*creaked, gleamed, whispered*) and one or two short lines of punctuated dialogue lifts Language marks dramatically.

Always double-check that you copied the prompt’s exact opening sentence smoothly into Paragraph 1 and checked past-tense verbs, commas, and quotation marks across every paragraph.

questions.questionText:
Write a composition on: 'The importance of keeping our community clean.'
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Expository Composition Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Structure **"The importance of keeping our community clean"** across 4 cohesive paragraphs: **(1) Introduction:** Define a clean community environment (litter-free streets, unblocked drains, clean water points, trimmed verges) and state clearly that environmental cleanliness protects public health, safety, and civic pride [4 marks]. **(2) Body Paragraph 1 — Health & Disease Prevention:** Explain concretely how clearing rotting waste and stagnant puddles destroys breeding places for **houseflies, rats, and malaria mosquitoes**, dramatically cutting cholera, typhoid, and diarrhoea outbreaks among young children [6 marks]. **(3) Body Paragraph 2 — Safety, Environment & Pride:** Detail how proper bins and avoiding burning plastic keep air breathable, prevent plastic litter from choking livestock or storm drains, protect streams from runoff pollution, and make markets and schools welcoming for visitors [6 marks]. **(4) Conclusion — Practical Actions:** Call on households, youth clubs, and councils to practise *Reduce–Reuse–Recycle*, compost organic scraps, and join monthly national clean-up days [9 marks for structure & language accuracy].

Expository essays earn top ZIMSEC marks through **clear logical topic sentences** (*"First and most urgently, a clean neighbourhood safeguards every family’s health..."*) paired with real Zimbabwean illustrations rather than repetitive empty slogans (*"Cleanliness is good, keep clean"*).

Check spelling of tricky environmental words (**environment, hygiene, mosquitoes, diarrhoea, community, responsibility**) and avoid informal second-person lecturing (*"You must stop littering!"*)—prefer inclusive civic voice (*"Every resident and learner shares a duty to..."*).

questions.questionText:
Write a story ending with: 'From that day onwards, I understood the value of telling the truth.'
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Narrative Composition Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Plan a realistic storyline that builds naturally toward the required final sentence: **"From that day onwards, I understood the value of telling the truth."** **Paragraph 1 (Setup & Temptation):** Introduce a believable school or home incident—for example, accidentally cracking a classmate’s science thermos or losing textbook money—and yielding briefly to fear by blaming someone else or staying silent [5 marks]. **Paragraph 2 (Tension & Consequence):** Describe the guilt eating at your conscience as an innocent friend gets scolded or worried adults search tirelessly, showing physical details (*knot in stomach, sleepless night, avoiding eyes*) [8 marks]. 

**Paragraph 3 (Turning Point & Confession):** Show courage stepping forward to admit the honest truth privately to the teacher or parent, describing their firm yet respectful response because you confessed willingly (*Unhu/Ubuntu* integrity) [6 marks]. **Paragraph 4 (Conclusion):** Finish smoothly by placing the exact closing prompt word-for-word at the very end (*"From that day onwards, I understood the value of telling the truth."*) [6 marks].

Ending-sentence narratives fail most often when writers race through the whole story and tack the required closing sentence onto an unrelated ending like a sticker. Weaving guilt, honesty, and forgiveness steadily throughout Paragraphs 2 and 3 makes the closing line land powerfully and earn high Content & Style marks.

Check speech punctuation if including dialogue (*"Please forgive me, Sir..."*) and verify the closing sentence matches the prompt verbatim.

questions.questionText:
Write an article for your school magazine about responsible use of mobile phones.
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**School Magazine Article Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Follow **Magazine Article Layout**: **(1) Catchy Title & Author Byline:** e.g., **"Smart Screens, Smart Minds: Using Mobile Phones Responsibly at School"** *By Tariro Ncube, Grade 7 Green* [3 marks]; **(2) Engaging Hook Introduction:** Acknowledge how mobile phones have transformed modern communication while asking whether smartphones help or harm primary learners’ studies [3 marks]; **(3) Balanced Body Paragraphs:** Paragraph 2 highlights genuine **educational benefits** when guided by adults (accessing offline study apps, ZIMSEC past papers, digital dictionaries, and emergency family safety contact). Paragraph 3 examines **real risks of misuse** (gaming/social media addiction cutting sleep and revision time, classroom distraction, cyberbullying, and eye strain) [12 marks]; **(4) Conclusion & Golden Guidelines:** Propose clear school-friendly rules—keeping phones silent/switched off during lessons, balancing screen time with outdoor sport/reading books, and seeking parent guidance online [7 marks].

Magazine articles use a lively, semi-formal journalistic tone written directly for fellow learners, teachers, and parents—engaging readers with rhetorical questions (*"Does your phone run your evening, or do you manage your time?"*) without slipping into SMS abbreviations (*u, plz, lol*).

Never format a magazine article as a formal letter with *"Dear Sir"* or *"Yours faithfully"*—keep **Headline + Byline → Engaging Hook → Balanced Pros & Cons → Practical Advice** cleanly.

questions.questionText:
Write a dialogue between two learners planning a community clean-up campaign.
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Dialogue Format & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Set the scene briefly in 1–2 present-tense stage notes *(Setting: Under the mango tree at school during break time. Chido and Farai are sketching plans for Friday’s clean-up.)* [3 marks]. Format every spoken turn strictly along the **left margin with speaker names in capitals/bold followed by a colon**—and **ZERO quotation marks** around dialogue lines [4 marks]:
**Chido:** Did you see how much plastic litter blew against the netball fence after yesterday’s wind?
**Farai:** I noticed it too! Why don’t we ask Mrs Moyo for gloves and sacks so Grade 7 can lead a clean-up campaign?
Across **8–10 natural exchanges**, cover **(a) naming the litter problem**, **(b) gathering tools/volunteers and delegating roles** (separating recyclables from compostable leaves), **(c) safety/hygiene precautions (gloves, washing hands)**, and **(d) keeping bins tidy permanently** [18 marks for plot progression, natural tone, and accurate mechanics].

Natural dialogues sound like real courteous Zimbabwean learners conversing—using contractions naturally inside spoken lines (*"Let’s ask...", "That’s brilliant!"*), brief action brackets *(pointing toward the gate)*, and balanced speaking turns rather than giant five-sentence monologues by one speaker.

The #1 ZIMSEC dialogue error is putting **'"..."' quotation marks** around spoken script lines alongside 'Name:'. In play/dialogue script format, the speaker name + colon replaces speech marks completely!

questions.questionText:
Write a speech to your school assembly on the importance of reading.
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Speech Format & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Open with a courteous **Zimbabwean school assembly salutation** moving cleanly down rank order: *"The School Head, Deputy Head, teachers, and fellow learners, good morning."* [3 marks]. **Paragraph 1 (Hook & Purpose):** Capture attention immediately (*"Imagine unlocking a doorway that lets you travel to Great Zimbabwe, explore distant planets, or master any examination—all without leaving your wooden desk! That magic key is reading."*) [4 marks]. **Paragraphs 2–3 (Three Developed Reasons):** Develop **(1) richer vocabulary, spelling, and English composition fluency**; **(2) stronger comprehension across Science, Mathematics, and Heritage subjects**; and **(3) inspiring stories building empathy, imagination, and peaceful relaxation** instead of idle screen scrolling [11 marks]. **Paragraph 4 (Call to Action & Thank You):** Challenge peers to borrow one library book weekly and establish silent evening reading circles, closing politely with **"Thank you very much for listening."** [7 marks].

A written speech relies on warm, spoken persuasion using **first-person plural pronouns ("we", "our", "let us")**, clear signposting (*"First...", "Even more importantly..."*), and short memorable closing challenges tailored to a live audience standing at morning assembly.

Do NOT add letter addresses at the top of a speech, and never forget the formal greeting (*"The Head, teachers, and fellow learners..."*) and closing *"Thank you."*

questions.questionText:
Write a report on a school sports day held at your school.
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**School Sports Day Report Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Begin strictly with a **Formal Report Header**: **TO:** The School Head | **FROM:** Tendai Mupfumi (Sports Captain) | **DATE:** 25 October 2026 | **SUBJECT:** Report on the 2026 Inter-House School Sports Day [4 marks]. **Paragraph 1 (Introduction & Overview):** State concisely *when* and *where* the event occurred (Friday 23 October on the school athletics field), *who attended* (all four houses, parents, teachers, neighbouring headteachers), and the overall aim [4 marks]. **Paragraph 2 (Activities & Participation):** Summarise factually the opening march-past, track events (100 m, 200 m, 4×100 m relays), field jumps/throws, and enthusiastic house cheering with fair play [6 marks]. 

**Paragraph 3 (Results & Recommendations):** Report objective highlights (e.g., *Nyathi House won the overall trophy with 420 points, breaking two Grade 7 sprint records; minor heat fatigue was handled swiftly by the clinic club*) and conclude with **two constructive recommendations** (adding shaded water tents and repairing two long-jump pit boards before next season) signed *"Report compiled by..."* [11 marks].

Report prose must sound **objective, clear, factual, and past-tense** without overly emotional exclamation marks or informal chat. Clearly separate what actually happened (**Findings/Events**) from practical improvements (**Recommendations**).

Avoid writing *"Yours faithfully"* (that belongs only to letters!) and never forget **TO / FROM / DATE / SUBJECT** at the very top.

questions.questionText:
Write a composition entitled: 'A journey I will never forget.'
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Descriptive/Narrative Composition Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Choose one vivid, realistic journey you know well—such as travelling early morning through mist over Birchenough Bridge, crossing the Eastern Highlands toward Mutare/Nyanga, or taking a holiday bus to grandparents in Masvingo near Great Zimbabwe. **Paragraph 1 (Departure & Purpose):** Set the dawn departure atmosphere cleanly (loading woven bags onto the bus roof, cool crisp morning air, crisp excitement and reason for the trip) [4 marks]. **Paragraphs 2–3 (Sensory Journey & Turning Incident):** Paint roadside sights (msasa hillsides in copper spring leaves, roadside craft stalls, winding mountain passes) and include **one memorable realistic event** along the way—helping a stranded motorist, spotting giraffes beside a highway reserve, or sharing a rainy breakdown turned lively by passengers singing together [13 marks]. **Paragraph 4 (Arrival & Reflection):** Describe arriving warmly at your destination and reflect thoughtfully on why that journey reshaped how you view Zimbabwe and kindness toward travellers [8 marks].

Strong travel essays balance **sensory description** (colours, smells of roasted mealies, engine hum) with **clear chronological pacing** rather than turning into a dull hour-by-hour timetable (*"At 08:00 we passed town X; at 09:00 we ate bread"*).

Maintain steady simple past tense throughout and vary transition connectors (*"Hours later...", "As the coach climbed steeply..."*) for smooth reading flow.

questions.questionText: Write a formal letter to your school head requesting a school vegetable garden. Explain its benefits and how it could be maintained.
questions.explanation:
**Formal Letter Plan & Model Guide [20 marks]:** Use **Two-Address Formal Letter Format**: top right carries your own school address and date; left margin below carries *The Head, [School Name], P.O. Box ...*; followed by **"Dear Sir/Madam,"** and a bold underlined subject line (**RE: REQUEST TO ESTABLISH A SCHOOL VEGETABLE GARDEN**). **Paragraph 1:** Politely introduce yourself on behalf of the Grade 7 Environmental/Agriculture Club and state the clear purpose of requesting a fenced unused corner plot behind the classrooms for a vegetable bed project.

**Paragraph 2 (Benefits & Sustainability):** Explain three concrete benefits cleanly—producing fresh covo, tomatoes, and onions to enrich school feeding meals (*nutritious balanced diet*), giving learners hands-on **Agric, Science & Technology** practice in composting, mulching, and *Pfumvudza* water conservation, and raising small income from surplus bunches for stationery/tools. 

**Paragraph 3 (Maintenance Plan & Formal Sign-Off):** Reassure the Head with a structured maintenance rota (morning watering rosters before assembly, rabbit/chicken wire fencing using club contributions, natural ash/marigold pest control, and teacher supervision during holidays), ending respectfully with **"Yours faithfully,"** and your full name.

Never omit the second (recipient’s) address or forget the **RE:** heading line, and always keep formal polite phrasing (*"I humbly request...", "We guarantee..."*)—never informal chat or *"Yours affectionately."*

questions.questionText: Write a composition about a day when you helped a stranger. Describe what happened, how you helped and what you learnt.
questions.explanation:
**Narrative Composition Plan & Model Guide [20 marks]:** Structure **"A day when I helped a stranger"** into four focused chronological paragraphs using vivid past-tense English. **Paragraph 1 (Meeting & Problem):** Set a believable Saturday morning scene—walking home from market shops or waiting at a rural clinic—when you notice an elderly stranger or worried young mother in genuine need (e.g., an elderly gogo’s heavy sack split open scattering maize meal across gravel, or a lost tourist searching for the main clinic).

**Paragraph 2 (Action & Kindness):** Describe step-by-step how you stepped in respectfully without expecting payment: kneeling swiftly to scoop clean grain into your spare shopping bag, carrying her load safely along the dusty path to the bus rank, or guiding a visitor politely to the duty nurse while offering cool drinking water. 

**Paragraph 3 (Gratitude & Lesson Learnt):** Capture the stranger’s genuine thankfulness and reflect clearly on what the moment taught you about ***Unhu/Ubuntu***, courage, and noticing quiet neighbours in need—making small acts of helpfulness deeply rewarding.

**Examiner Guidance:** Avoid far-fetched superhero rescues; ZIMSEC Grade 7 markers reward warm, everyday realistic kindness told with crisp sensory details and clean past-tense verb control.

questions.questionText: Write a speech encouraging learners to protect trees around the school. Give at least three practical actions.
questions.explanation:
**Speech Plan & Model Guide [20 marks]:** Open with a clear formal assembly greeting: *"The School Head, respected teachers, and dear fellow learners, good morning."* **Paragraph 1 (Importance of Trees):** State your persuasive theme immediately—trees are the green lungs of our school, giving cool study shade during scorching October afternoons, sheltering birds, anchoring soil against heavy gully erosion, and enriching fresh oxygen.

**Paragraph 2 (Three Practical Learner Actions):** Present three specific actions pupils can start today: **(1) Adopt-a-Sapling Teams**, where each class plants and waters one hardy indigenous or fruit tree (guava, acacia, msasa) with mulch basins around the roots; **(2) Protect Young Bark & Branches**, strictly stopping swinging on saplings, carving initials into trunks, or breaking live twigs for play; and **(3) Practise Paper Recycling & Clean Firewood Habits**, cutting wasteful exercise-book tearing and clearing dry dead branches responsibly instead of cutting living trees. 

**Paragraph 3 (Closing Challenge):** Remind peers that *"One learner, one thriving tree"* transforms bare dusty yards into green legacy gardens, closing politely with **"Thank you very much."**

Remember speech voice uses **"we", "us", "let us"** directly toward live listeners—avoid turning a speech into a silent essay or writing letter addresses.

questions.questionText: Write a report to your head teacher about a lost-and-found incident at school. Include the time, place, action taken and recommendations.
questions.explanation:
**School Lost-and-Found Report Guide [20 marks]:** Format strictly as an official **ZIMSEC Report**: **TO:** The Head Teacher | **FROM:** [Your Full Name, Grade 7 Prefect] | **DATE:** [Date] | **SUBJECT:** Report on Lost-and-Found Sports Bag Incident. **Paragraph 1 (Time, Place & Discovery):** State factually that on Wednesday afternoon around 1:15 p.m. near the Grade 6 bicycle shed, you spotted an unattended navy backpack containing a calculator, ZIMSEC revision book, and $15 in an envelope.

**Paragraph 2 (Action Taken):** Detail transparent, honest custody steps taken immediately: without opening pockets further, you left the bag untouched in content, asked fellow monitor Tariro to witness the hand-over, delivered the bag safely to the Senior Teacher on Duty’s locked office, logged a brief item description in the school lost-property register, and watched assembly announcement verify the rightful Grade 5 owner cleanly the next morning. 

**Paragraph 3 (Recommendations):** Propose two clear preventative measures—labelling all bags and stationery clearly with permanent markers at term start, and placing a dedicated lockable Lost-and-Found cabinet near reception—signed formally *"Submitted by [Full Name]"*.

Keep report language calm, factual, third-person/objective, and strictly in past tense—never add casual greetings or *"Yours sincerely."*

questions.questionText: Describe a memorable visit to a tourist attraction in Zimbabwe. Include the journey, what you saw and what you learnt.
questions.explanation:
**Descriptive Composition Guide — Visiting a Zimbabwean Tourist Attraction [20 marks]:** Pick a real national treasure you can describe richly—such as **Victoria Falls (*Mosi-oa-Tunya*)**, **Great Zimbabwe Ruins**, **Matobo Hills**, **Nyanga Mountains**, or **Chinhoyi Caves**. **Paragraph 1 (The Journey):** Set out at dawn by school bus or family car, capturing changing rural landscapes, acacia hills, cheerful songs onboard, and mounting excitement as welcome signposts appear.

**Paragraph 2 (What You Saw & Experienced):** Paint vivid sensory details—the rising white mist and roaring thunder of Victoria Falls soaking visitors along Rainforest walkways, or monumental dry-stone granite enclosures climbing hills at Great Zimbabwe—alongside knowledgeable guides explaining indigenous heritage and local woodcarvers’ markets. 

**Paragraph 3 (What You Learnt):** Conclude thoughtfully explaining what you discovered about Zimbabwe’s geological wonders, pre-colonial engineering, wildlife conservation, and why tourism jobs require every citizen to protect natural shrines from litter and vandalism.

Include **accurate local geographic details** and crisp sensory imagery (sound, mist, granite colour, birdsong) rather than generic statements like *"it was very nice and we ate food."*

questions.questionText: Write an informal letter to a relative thanking them for helping you with your school work.
questions.explanation:
**Informal Letter Plan & Model Guide [20 marks]:** Use **Single-Address Friendly Format** (your own home/school address + date at top right; warm greeting *"Dear Auntie Rudo,"* or *"Dear Uncle Farai,"* on the left). **Paragraph 1 (Warm Greeting & Reason):** Ask kindly after your relative’s health and family, then immediately state your heartfelt purpose—writing to express sincere gratitude for the patient evening coaching in Mathematics fractions and buying your Grade 7 Science revision pack.

**Paragraph 2 (Impact & Progress):** Describe clearly how their patient encouragement boosted your confidence: share a specific improvement—jumping from 54% to 82% in mock paper tests, mastering long division without panic, and helping younger siblings read aloud nicely at home—showing their sacrifice truly bore fruit. 

**Paragraph 3 (Update & Warm Sign-off):** Promise to keep working diligently toward top Grade 7 ZIMSEC results, share brief joyful news of school activities, and close affectionately with *"Your grateful niece/nephew, [First Name only]."*

Match warm respectful family tone suited to an elder relative (*Uncle/Auntie*)—courteous and grateful without slang like *"Hey bro!"* or overly stiff business words like *"Yours faithfully."*

questions.questionText: Write a story beginning: 'The moment the lights went out, everyone became silent.'
questions.explanation:
**Narrative Composition Plan & Model Guide [20 marks]:** Open **verbatim** with: **"The moment the lights went out, everyone became silent."** **Paragraph 1 (Setting & Instant Tension):** Establish a quiet evening scene—say, evening Grade 7 boarding study prep or a stormy night indoors watching the end of a family story—when thunder snaps overhead and pitch darkness floods every corner of the hall simultaneously.

**Paragraph 2 (Action & Resolution):** Describe believable physical reactions in the dark—chairs scraping softly, someone fumbling calmly for a solar lantern/torch, a prefect reassuring younger peers to stay seated safely rather than rushing doorways in panic, and the glowing warm beam of candles turning anxious tension into cheerful calm conversation or singing while rain taps roof iron. 

**Paragraph 3 (Return of Power & Reflection):** When solar/power clicks back warmly twenty minutes later, show everyone laughing kindly and concluding what staying calm under sudden surprises taught the group about teamwork and level-headedness.

**Examiner Guidance:** Never rely on cheap horror ghosts or waking from a dream—grounded realistic human reactions earn the highest ZIMSEC Content and Style scores.

questions.questionText: Write a speech to be delivered at assembly about the importance of punctuality.
questions.explanation:
**Assembly Speech Guide — Importance of Punctuality [20 marks]:** Begin properly: *"The Head, Deputy Head, teachers, and fellow learners, good morning."* **Paragraph 1 (Hook & Definition):** Explain crisply what **punctuality** means—arriving on time before the morning bell, submitting homework promptly, and honouring scheduled lessons—before asking what happens when one latecomer bursts noisily into class mid-lesson.

**Paragraph 2 (Three Reasons Punctuality Matters):** Develop **(1) Respect for Others’ Time**—interrupting morning devotions or Mathematics instructions steals learning minutes from forty waiting classmates; **(2) Building Academic Calm & Success**—settling desks five minutes early prevents rushed forgotten pens and exam panic; and **(3) Preparing Future Character**—doctors, drivers, farmers, and engineers depend daily on reliability and self-discipline. 

**Paragraph 3 (Action Plan):** Encourage practical morning habits—packing satchels and polishing uniforms the night before and setting out fifteen minutes early—ending warmly with **"Thank you for your attention."**

Write rhythmically as spoken persuasion (*"Look around your morning desk...", "Let us start tomorrow..."*) so the assembly speech reads convincingly aloud.

questions.questionText: Write a report about a sports day held at your school. Include activities, participation, results and recommendations.
questions.explanation:
**Sports Day Report Guide [20 marks]:** Structure clearly with formal header (**TO: The Head Teacher | FROM: [Your Full Name, Sports Secretary] | DATE: [Date] | SUBJECT: Report on the Annual Inter-House School Sports Day**). **Paragraph 1 (Overview & Participation):** Log date, venue, participating houses (e.g., *Eagle, Lion, Buffalo, Kudu*), turnout of parents/community, and smooth opening march-past.

**Paragraph 2 (Activities & Official Results):** Summarise key track/field disciplines cleanly (sprints, relays, long jump, netball/football friendlies) alongside crisp factual outcomes—for example, *Kudu House captured 1st place overall with 385 points, closely followed by Eagle House (360 points); Grade 7 relay teams recorded strong sportsmanship with zero disqualifications*. 

**Paragraph 3 (Observations & Recommendations):** Note two strengths (enthusiastic participation, prompt first-aid support) plus two practical improvements for next year (re-marking faded lane chalk earlier and adding extra shaded water jugs at the finish line), signed professionally at bottom.

**Examiner Guidance:** Maintain crisp factual past-tense reporting—keep personal boasting out and balance praise fairly with practical logistical recommendations.

questions.questionText: Write a composition explaining how your community can prepare for floods.
questions.explanation:
**Expository Composition Guide — Preparing Your Community for Floods [20 marks]:** **Paragraph 1 (Introduction):** Define seasonal **flash floods and river overflows** caused by heavy Cyclone or summer cloudbursts across Zimbabwe, stating clearly that early community planning saves human lives, livestock, and precious harvests.

**Paragraph 2 (Three Practical Preparation Measures):** Explain **(1) Clearing Storm Drains, Culverts & Waterways** before October rains so rushing runoff flows harmlessly instead of bursting into homes; **(2) Relocating Homes/Kraals Away from Low River Floodplains & Elevating Grain/Seed Stores** onto raised brick platforms above damp flood lines while storing waterproof emergency kits (torches, dry food, clinic records, water-purification tablets); and **(3) Community Early-Warning Alerts & Safe Evacuation Routes** where village heads/schools share weather bulletins and rehearse moving children, elders, and cattle to high ground *before* rivers rise dangerously.

**Paragraph 3 (Conclusion — Golden Rule & Unity):** Conclude urgently with the lifesaving rule **"Never cross flooded low-level bridges or fast brown rivers on foot or by bus"**, showing how disciplined cooperation protects whole villages through storm seasons.

questions.questionText: Write a formal letter to a local organisation requesting support for a school reading club.
questions.explanation:
**Formal Letter Plan — Requesting Reading Club Support [20 marks]:** Apply strict **Two-Address Formal Format** (your school’s address/date top right; left margin recipient address e.g., *The Director, [Local Business / Book Trust], Harare*; **"Dear Sir/Madam,"**; bold subject heading **RE: REQUEST FOR BOOK DONATION SUPPORT FOR OUR SCHOOL READING CLUB**). **Paragraph 1:** Introduce your school’s newly launched 40-member Reading Club respectfully, explaining learners’ keen hunger to improve English comprehension and general knowledge despite severe shortages of age-appropriate storybooks.

**Paragraph 2 (Specific Need & Impact):** Specify exactly what support would help—used or new primary storybooks, encyclopedias, ZIMSEC reference dictionaries, or sturdy wooden shelves—and illustrate clearly how 100 shared books can rotate cleanly among all Grade 5–7 classes during lunch breaks and weekend reading circles, lifting literacy scores and protecting youths from idle habits. 

**Paragraph 3 (Accountability & Polite Close):** Promise careful book-lending tracking, protective plastic book covers, and a termly thank-you progress letter before closing formally with **"Yours faithfully,"**, signature, and full printed name.

questions.questionText: Write a story about a mistake that taught you an important lesson.
questions.explanation:
**Narrative Composition Plan — A Mistake That Taught an Important Lesson [20 marks]:** **Paragraph 1 (Situation & Poor Choice):** Introduce a realistic mistake driven by impatience or carelessness—for instance, rushing out to play football before locking the backyard chicken coop or copying a friend’s homework/ignoring an adult safety rule about cycling without working brakes.

**Paragraph 2 (Immediate Consequence):** Describe vividly what went wrong when that shortcut backfired—stray dogs frightening prized hens, or skidding awkwardly onto a gravel verge grazing your knee and bending the front wheel—highlighting panic, regret, and honest embarrassment as family members rushed to help fix the damage cleanly. 

**Paragraph 3 (Lesson & Changed Behaviour):** Show yourself apologising sincerely, helping repair the mess/earn back trust over the following weeks, and ending thoughtfully with how one painful afternoon taught lasting responsibility (*measuring consequences before acting in haste*).

**Examiner Guidance:** Remember: strong narratives examine *why* the mistake happened, genuine feelings afterward, and concrete growth—not merely *"I made a mistake, sorry, the end."*
